title: A rare case of tumefactive demyelination of brain: A case report and literature review
case_prompt: A 30-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 3-day fever followed 6 days later by fluent but non-meaningful speech, word-finding difficulty, comprehension deficits, and impaired repetition consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. She remained fully conscious, with no focal motor or sensory deficits. Vital signs were normal except for a temperature of 38.5°C. Routine blood tests, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), an extensive autoimmune screen (including ANA, extractable nuclear antigens, dsDNA, ANCA), and serum ACE were all within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed mild diffusion restriction at the periphery of lesions on FLAIR and T2-weighted sequences and, after gadolinium administration, no enhancement. Gradient echo and susceptibility-weighted sequences were not performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a protein level of 54 mg/dL, glucose of 50 mg/dL, 60 cells/mm3 (60% polymorphonuclear, 40% lymphocytes), and six oligoclonal bands in CSF with none in serum; no organisms were seen. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated normal levels of N-acetyl aspartate, creatine, choline, and lactate in the affected regions.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious and inflammatory conditions (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, malignancies) were deemed unlikely — “there was low suspicion for various infectious and inflammatory differentials such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and malignancies.”  
2. Active inflammation or vascular lesions were excluded by the absence of enhancement — “gadolinium contrast administration showed no enhancement, indicating the absence of active inflammation or vascular changes in the brain.”  
3. Brain tumors and abscesses were ruled out by peripheral rather than central diffusion restriction — “Our patient had mild diffusion at the edges or periphery. This helped us to exclude tumors and abscesses.”  
4. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) was considered less likely given the lack of a post-infective origin — “In contrast to acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), tumefactive demyelinating lesions typically do not have a post-infective origin.”  
5. Multiple sclerosis was unlikely to manifest as a solitary initial tumefactive lesion progressing to MS — “people who first show up with a single tumefactive demyelinating lesion rarely go on to get MS.”  
6. A neoplastic process was deemed improbable based on a normal spectroscopic profile — “MRS reveals normal metabolite levels in affected brain regions, providing clarity on NAA, creatine, choline, and lactate concentrations.”
